title: Diagnostic Accuracy Masks Outdated Reasoning: Evaluating LLMs on Evolving Clinical Guidelines
content: Large language models (LLMs) in clinical decision support must apply current rather than superseded definitions, but existing evaluation methods rarely distinguish a correct conclusion reached via a valid rationale from one that relies on outdated vocabulary. We tested four open-weight LLMs (7–23.6 billion parameters, three model families) on 45 physician-reviewed sepsis vignettes and conceptual questions under three conditions: a full five-document guideline corpus mixing current (Sepsis-3) and superseded (SIRS-based) definitions, access restricted via static retrieval pruning, and no corpus access. A deterministic lexical tracker measured superseded- and current-guideline vocabulary density, avoiding LLM-as-judge grading biases; because the tracker captures surface terminology use rather than clinical endorsement or diagnostic error, we assessed diagnostic conclusion correctness independently. Four findings emerged. First, injecting guideline context of any kind increased superseded-vocabulary use for every model relative to the no-context baseline. Second, narrowing this context through static retrieval pruning produced model-dependent effects rather than a uniform benefit: superseded-vocabulary use fell significantly for an 8-billion-parameter model, rose significantly for a 23.6-billion-parameter model, and did not differ significantly for the remaining two models; for the 20-billion-parameter model, this null result remains statistically undetermined rather than demonstrated absent. Third, three models maintained high (89–100%) conclusion accuracy across conditions, but one biomedically fine-tuned model showed a severe, distractor-driven accuracy collapse, falling to 17.9–25.0% under injected context. Finally, correct final answers substantially overstated the clinical validity of the models’ stated rationale: a blinded physician review, corroborated by a second independent reviewer, found the stated clinical rationale valid in only 53.7% of responses despite near-ceiling conclusion accuracy, chiefly reflecting quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA)-as-diagnostic and lactate-as-organ-dysfunction conflations. Together, these findings indicate that context restriction’s effect on superseded-vocabulary use is model-dependent rather than a general safeguard, and that correct final answers can substantially overstate the clinical validity of a language model’s stated rationale.
